```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Once a document is cut into chunks, something has to decide how the model works
through them. Send everything at once? Ask each chunk separately and combine the
answers? Find the few chunks most like the question and ignore the rest? These
are *reading strategies*, which harnessr calls *readers*. They decide most of the
cost of a run and much of the quality of its answer. The same chunks read two
ways can take one request or dozens, and can find a fact or miss it.

This guide explains each reader in plain terms, shows how they differ on the same
document, and gives a way to choose. `vignette("harnessr")` introduces the
package and its ideas.

## Setting up

The examples use a stand-in for a real model, so they run for free. This one
answers each kind of request the way a model would: it scores an excerpt when
asked to score and quotes when asked to quote, so every reader can do its normal
work. You do not need to follow its details; it plays the part of the model.

```{r message = FALSE}
library(harnessr)
old <- gr_options(verbose = FALSE, embedder = "lexical")

stand_in <- function(messages, params) {
  instructions <- messages[[1]]$content
  everything <- paste(vapply(messages, function(m) m$content, character(1)),
                      collapse = "\n")
  task <- if (is.null(params$schema_name)) "" else params$schema_name
  if (task == "relevance") {        # rerank: score one excerpt from 0 to 10
    excerpt <- messages[[length(messages)]]$content
    if (grepl("revenue", excerpt, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
      return('{"score": 9, "reason": "States revenue."}')
    }
    return('{"score": 2, "reason": "About something else."}')
  }
  if (task == "iterative_step") {   # iterative: can I answer yet?
    return('{"can_answer": true, "answer": "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.", "next_query": ""}')
  }
  if (task == "reading_plan") {     # preview: which sections to read
    return('{"sections": [{"id": 1, "treatment": "read", "reason": "States revenue."}]}')
  }
  if (grepl("You extract evidence", instructions, fixed = TRUE)) {   # skim: quote
    quote <- regmatches(everything,
                        regexpr("[^.\n]*revenue of [0-9.]+ million dollars[^.\n]*", everything))
    return(if (length(quote)) quote else "NONE")
  }
  "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars."
}
```

`embedder = "lexical"` makes the readers that search for similar text use simple
word matching instead of a paid embedding service; more on that below.

Now the document, cut into chunks along its section headings:

```{r}
chunks <- gr_segment(gr_ingest(gr_example()),
                     list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120))
gr_chunk_stats(chunks)
```

Eight chunks. A real report would have hundreds, and the differences below would
be correspondingly larger.

## Listing the readers

```{r}
gr_readers()[, c("name", "signature", "cost_calls")]
```

`cost_calls` is how many requests a reader makes, as a formula in **N**, the
number of chunks. A reader whose count grows with N makes a hundred times as
many requests on a document a hundred times longer. But you pay for tokens, not
requests, and a reader that looks at every chunk sends every token: `stuff`
makes one request whatever the length, yet that request carries the whole
document, so its cost grows with the document too. Each request also repeats
the instructions and writes its own reply, so among readers that see everything,
more requests cost more. The readers that look at a selection of chunks (the
`topk` ones below) cost roughly the same however long the document is.

`signature` describes how a reader works, in three parts separated by `|`:

- **which chunks it looks at**: `all` of them; the `topk` most relevant; the
  `head` (opening) of the document; the chunks a `planned` reading chose; or, for
  an `ensemble`, whatever its members looked at;
- **how many requests it makes**, the same formula in short;
- **what carries over between requests**: `none` (each request stands alone),
  `tree` (answers are combined in stages), or `forward` (each request builds on
  the one before).

The built-in readers all have different signatures, and `ensemble` refuses
members that share one: two readers with the same signature would be the same
method under two names.

## Every reader on one document

Here is the same question put to the same eight chunks by each general-purpose
reader. `extract` and `screen` are left out: they are built for literature
reviews and need a schema or criteria.

```{r}
read_with <- function(reader) {
  model <- gr_mock_client(stand_in)
  ans <- gr_read(chunks, "What was revenue in 2024?", model, reader)
  data.frame(reader = reader, requests = length(model$calls()),
             chunks_used = length(ans$chunks_used), partial = ans$partial)
}
readers <- c("stuff", "map_reduce", "refine", "skim", "hierarchical",
             "retrieve", "rerank", "iterative", "preview", "ensemble")
do.call(rbind, lapply(readers, read_with))
```

The stand-in gives every reader the same answer, and none of the runs degraded
(`partial` is `FALSE`). What differs is the work: from one request to eleven for
eight chunks, and from reading everything to relying on a single passage. On a
long document the gap widens: the number of requests grows with the document for
some readers and not at all for others, and the cost grows for every reader that
reads the whole document.

## The readers

### `stuff`: everything in one request

Puts the whole document into a single prompt. It is the simplest reader, and
usually the cheapest way to have the model read all of a document, with one set
of instructions and one reply. Its cost still grows with the document's length.
The model sees everything at once, so it can connect facts from different
places. The limit is the context window: if the document does not fit,
`stuff` sends what fits, warns, and marks the answer partial
(`on_overflow = "error"` makes it stop instead). Very long prompts also dilute
attention; details in the middle of a long prompt are more easily missed.

**Use it for** documents comfortably inside the model's context window.
**Recipe:** `"fast"`, which `answer_document()` uses by default for a document
of up to 50,000 tokens, or less on a model with a small context window.

### `map_reduce`: every chunk separately, then combined

Asks the question of each chunk on its own ("map"), then combines the answers in
stages ("reduce"). Nothing is skipped, each request is small, and the per-chunk
requests can run in parallel. It costs N requests plus the combining steps, and a
fact that only makes sense across two chunks can be missed, because no single
request sees both.

**Use it for** questions where every mention matters: "list every risk named in
this report". **Recipe:** `"thorough"`, which `answer_document()` uses by
default for a longer document.

### `refine`: a draft revised chunk by chunk

Reads the chunks in order, keeping a running answer and revising it with each new
chunk. Later text can correct earlier conclusions, which suits documents whose
argument develops. It costs N requests that cannot run in parallel, and the
running answer can drift.

**Use it for** narratives and arguments that build. **Recipe:** `"narrative"`.

### `skim`: quote first, then answer

For each chunk, asks the model to copy out any passages that bear on the
question, then answers once from those passages alone. The final answer rests on
quotations, which harnessr checks against the text (see below). It costs N + 1
requests; the per-chunk step can use a cheaper model through `skim_model`.

**Use it for** questions where you want the answer tied to exact wording.
**Recipe:** `"precise"`.

### `hierarchical`: summaries of summaries

Summarises each chunk, then summarises groups of summaries (`fan_in` at a time),
level by level, until everything fits in one prompt, and answers from that. It
suits questions about a whole long document, such as "what is this report's
overall argument?", at the price of detail lost in summarising. `summary_model`
can use a cheaper model for the summaries; `max_levels` caps the depth.

**Use it for** long, structured documents where you want an overview.
**Recipe:** `"survey"`.

### `retrieve`: only the most relevant chunks

Turns the question and every chunk into *embeddings* (lists of numbers that
place similar text close together) and sends only the `top_k` chunks closest to
the question, in a single request. The cost of the answer does not grow with the
document, which makes it the usual choice for finding one fact in something long.
The risk: a chunk that answers the question but does not *look* like it is never
sent.

**Use it for** a specific fact in a long document. **Recipe:** `"needle"`.

### `rerank`: shortlist, then let the model judge

Makes a quick word-matching shortlist (`rerank_candidates` chunks, 20 by default),
asks the model to score each for relevance from 0 to 10, and answers from the
chunks scoring at least `rerank_min_score`. The model's judgement is better than
word matching, at the price of one scoring request per shortlisted chunk.
`skim_model` can do the scoring more cheaply.

If no chunk could be scored, for example because the provider does not support
the structured replies the scoring needs, it falls back to the word-matching
order and warns. If only some chunks were scored, the answer is marked partial.

**Use it for** long documents where word matching alone picks badly, including
scanned ones. **Recipe:** `"scanned"`.

### `iterative`: look, decide what is missing, look again

Retrieves a few chunks and asks the model whether it can answer yet, and if not,
what it should look for next. Then it retrieves again, up to `max_rounds` times. It
suits questions needing several facts from different places ("how did the drop in
margin affect the dividend?"). `ans$notes$queries` records what it searched for in
each round, and `ans$notes$stop_reason` why it stopped.

**Use it for** multi-step questions. **Recipe:** `"research"`.

### `preview`: plan, then read

Shows the model an outline of the document (section headings, sizes, and short
excerpts) and asks which sections to read in full, which to skim, and which to
skip. Then it reads accordingly. A section the plan does not mention is read, never
skipped, so silence cannot lose part of the document; the plan is recorded in
`ans$notes$plan`, so "sections 3 and 5 were not read" is visible. If no usable
plan comes back, it reads everything and marks the answer partial.

**Use it for** long documents with clear sections, when most of them are
irrelevant to the question.

### `ensemble`: several readers, compared

Runs two or more different readers (`members`; by default `retrieve` and
`map_reduce`) and asks the model to reconcile their answers. It costs the sum of
its members plus one request, and pays off when a wrong answer is expensive.
Members must have different signatures, because running the same method twice is
not a second opinion.

**Use it for** high-stakes questions. **Recipe:** `"consensus"`.

### `extract` and `screen`

`extract` fills in a table of details (a *schema*) from every chunk, and `screen`
decides whether a document meets a set of criteria. Both belong to the
literature-review workflow in `vignette("review")`.

## Choosing a reader

| your situation | reader | recipe | cost grows with document length? |
|---|---|---|---|
| the document fits comfortably in one request | `stuff` | `"fast"` | yes, though it is one request |
| one specific fact, long document | `retrieve` | `"needle"` | no (embeddings aside) |
| one fact, and word matching picks badly; scanned pages | `rerank` | `"scanned"` | no, fixed by `rerank_candidates` |
| every mention must be found | `map_reduce` | `"thorough"` | yes |
| the answer must rest on exact quotations; a short document with every sentence weighed | `skim` | `"precise"` | yes |
| an overview of a long document | `hierarchical` | `"survey"` | yes |
| an argument that develops through the text | `refine` | `"narrative"` | yes |
| several facts combined from different places | `iterative` | `"research"` | no, up to `max_rounds` (embeddings aside) |
| long document, most sections irrelevant | `preview` | none | depends on the plan |
| a wrong answer would be costly | `ensemble` | `"consensus"` | as its members |

If unsure, run two or three on a document where you already know the answer and
compare (see "Trying readers on your own documents" below).

## Recipes

A *recipe* names an ingestion, a segmentation and a reader together, with their
settings. The table above gives the recipe built on each reader. `gr_recipes()`
returns them all:

```{r}
do.call(rbind, lapply(names(gr_recipes()), function(n) {
  r <- gr_recipes(n)
  data.frame(recipe = n, segment = r$segment$method, reader = r$read$reader)
}))
```

`answer_document()` defaults to `"auto"`, which reads a document of up to 50,000
tokens (less on a model with a small context window) with `"fast"`, in one
request, and a longer one with `"thorough"`, one request per chunk. Both send
every chunk. `ans$recipe` says which was used. `gr_read_many()`, `gr_compare()`
and the review functions take one fixed recipe and refuse `"auto"`.

Printing a recipe shows every setting on all three steps:

```{r}
gr_recipes("thorough")
```

A recipe is a starting point. Any of its settings can be overridden by name in
the call, as in `answer_document(file, question, "needle", top_k = 3)`, and
`gr_recipe()` builds one from scratch (there is an example under "Trying readers
on your own documents" below).

`"legacy"` reproduces the previous release's behaviour (digit stripping,
3000-token paragraph chunks, no overlap), so you can measure the difference
rather than assume it.

## Choosing and placing chunks

`retrieve`, `rerank` and `iterative` choose which chunks the model sees. These
settings control the choice and where the chosen chunks go; each says which
readers it applies to.

**`top_k`** (`retrieve`, `rerank`, `iterative`) is how many chunks to send, 6 by
default. For `iterative` it is how many each round adds: the chunks gathered in
earlier rounds stay in the prompt as long as they fit. Too few and the answer
can be missed; too many and you pay for text that does not help.

**`min_score`** (`retrieve`) drops chunks less similar to the question than a
threshold, though the single best chunk is always kept.

**`mmr`** (`retrieve`, `iterative`) stops near-duplicates crowding each other
out. Plain top-k picks the chunks most like the question; if three paragraphs
say the same thing, all three get in. Below 1, `mmr` balances relevance against
similarity to what is already picked (0.7 is a reasonable start):

```{r}
repetitive <- paste(c(
  "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars in fiscal 2024.",
  "Total revenue reached 45.2 million dollars in the 2024 fiscal year.",
  "In fiscal 2024 the company recorded revenue of 45.2 million dollars.",
  "Headcount grew to 1,204 employees across nine clinical sites.",
  "The board approved a dividend of 0.42 dollars per share in March."),
  collapse = "\n\n")
pieces <- gr_segment(gr_ingest(repetitive), list(method = "paragraph", max_tokens = 40))
model <- gr_mock_client(stand_in)
picked <- function(mmr) {
  gr_read(pieces, "What was revenue?", model,
          list(reader = "retrieve", top_k = 3, mmr = mmr))$chunks_used
}
rbind("top-k (mmr = 1)" = picked(1), "mmr = 0.3" = picked(0.3))
```

Plain top-k spent all three places on the same fact; `mmr = 0.3` kept the best
one and used the other two for something different. It costs nothing extra.

**`context_order`** (`retrieve`, `rerank`, `iterative`) decides where the chosen
chunks sit in the prompt. Models attend best to the beginning and end of a long
prompt, so `"edges"` puts the best chunk first and the second-best last;
`"document"` keeps the order they appear in the document, which reads more
naturally when chunks are consecutive; the default `"relevance"` puts the best
first. It never changes which chunks were chosen, only where they sit.

**`restate`** (every reader but `extract` and `screen`) repeats the question
before the excerpts as well as after them, because a question asked once, after
several thousand tokens of text, is a long way from the start of the prompt.
`"auto"` does this when the text is long, `"always"` and `"never"` override.

Whether `mmr`, `context_order` or `restate` help depends on your documents and
model; test them rather than assume.

## Embeddings

`retrieve`, `iterative` and the `semantic` way of cutting chunks
(`vignette("segment")`) need *embeddings*. By default harnessr asks the model
provider for them, which costs a little and needs an internet connection.
`gr_options(embedder = "lexical")` uses word-matching vectors computed locally
instead: free, offline and exactly repeatable, but they match words rather than
meaning, so "turnover" will not find "revenue". Use lexical vectors for practice
and testing, and real embeddings for real work.

```{r}
gr_embedders()[, c("name", "deterministic", "description")]
```

## Reasoning effort, stage by stage

The default models reason before they answer. That reasoning is billed as
output and counts against the same cap as the reply, so it is part of what every
request costs. `effort` in `gr_read_spec()` sets how much of it to do: one value,
such as `"low"`, for every request, or a vector named by stage. It is sent only to
models harnessr lists as reasoning models (`gr_model_info(model)$reasoning`). By
default nothing is sent, and each request goes out at the provider's default.

Every request a reader makes carries a label naming its stage:

| reader | one request per chunk | the rest |
|---|---|---|
| `stuff` | none | `stuff.answer` |
| `map_reduce` | `map.answer` | `reduce` |
| `refine` | `refine.draft`, then `refine.revise` | none (the last revision is the answer) |
| `skim` | `skim.extract` | `skim.consolidate` (only if the passages do not fit), `skim.answer` |
| `hierarchical` | `hier.summarise.L1` | `hier.summarise.L2` and up, `hier.answer` |
| `retrieve` | none | `retrieve.answer` |
| `rerank` | `rerank.score` (each shortlisted chunk) | `rerank.answer` |
| `iterative` | none | `iterative.step` (one a round), `iterative.final` (only if no step could answer) |
| `preview` | `preview.skim` (each skimmed section) | `preview.plan`, `preview.answer` |
| `ensemble` | as its members | as its members, then `ensemble.adjudicate` |

The per-chunk requests are many and each does a small job, so they are where a
lower effort saves most; `?gr_read_spec` suggests a starting profile. A name
covers its own label and every label that starts with it and a dot, so `map`
covers `map.answer`, and an unnamed value covers the rest.

`gr_trace()` records every request a run makes. Here `map_reduce` reads the eight
chunks at low effort and merges at high:

```{r}
spec <- gr_read_spec("map_reduce", model = "gpt-5.6-luna",
                     effort = c(map = "low", reduce = "high"))
tr <- gr_trace()
ans <- gr_read(chunks, "What was revenue in 2024?", gr_mock_client(stand_in), spec,
               trace = tr)
with(as.data.frame(tr), table(stage, effort))
```

`model = "gpt-5.6-luna"` names a reasoning model: with the stand-in's own model
nothing would be sent, and the trace would have no `effort` column. A request at
`"high"` can spend the whole output cap reasoning and come back cut off, so give
it room with `max_answer_tokens`. `gr_compare()` (below) counts recipes that
differ only in effort as different, so you can test what a lower effort costs.
`vignette("runs")` covers effort across a literature review and what each trace
step records.

## Asking for citations

With `cite = TRUE` the model is asked to cite the chunks it used, as `[chunk 3]`.
Each chunk id leads back to a page and section through `ans$evidence`:

```{r}
citing <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params)
  "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars [chunk 2].")
ans <- gr_read(chunks, "What was revenue in 2024?", citing,
               list(reader = "stuff", cite = TRUE))
ans$answer
ans$evidence[ans$evidence$chunk_id == 2, c("chunk_id", "section")]
```

A citation to a chunk the model was never sent is caught and recorded in
`ans$notes$cited_unknown`, and marks the answer partial. `hierarchical` does not
support citations, because it answers from summaries rather than chunks.

## Checking what an answer rests on

`ans$evidence` holds different things depending on the reader:

| reader | `evidence$text` holds |
|---|---|
| `stuff`, `retrieve`, `rerank`, `iterative` | the chunks, word for word |
| `skim` | passages the model copied out |
| `map_reduce` | each chunk's answer |
| `refine`, `hierarchical` | nothing (the answer is built from drafts or summaries) |

Chunks sent word for word are true copies of the document by construction. The
passages `skim` collects are what the model *says* the document contains, so
harnessr checks every one against the chunk it came from:

```{r}
skimmed <- gr_read(chunks, "What was revenue in 2024?", gr_mock_client(stand_in), "skim")
gr_verify_evidence(skimmed)[, c("chunk_id", "verified", "match")]
```

Here is a model that invents one. The passage is fluent, on topic, attributed to
a real chunk, and not in the document, so it cannot be caught by eye:

```{r}
memo <- gr_segment(gr_ingest("Revenue rose to 45.2 million dollars.\n\nHeadcount grew to 1,204."),
                   list(method = "paragraph", max_tokens = 40))
inventing <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  if (grepl("You extract evidence", messages[[1]]$content, fixed = TRUE)) {
    return("Revenue rose to 88.9 billion dollars on record demand.")
  }
  "Revenue was 88.9 billion dollars."
})
invented <- gr_read(memo, "What was revenue?", inventing, "skim")
gr_verify_evidence(invented)[, c("kind", "verified", "match")]
invented$partial
```

`match` is 1 for an exact quotation once spacing, quote marks, dashes and
capitals are folded away, since a faithful quotation can differ in those. A
changed figure is not folded away. Below 1, `match` is the fraction of the
passage carried by its longest consecutive run in the source, so where a change
falls matters as much as how much changed: a changed last word leaves a run of
nine in ten and scores 0.9, while a changed word in the middle splits the
passage and scores about 0.5. Below about 0.3 there is no quotation left, only
shared vocabulary. A run is used rather than word overlap because overlap cannot
tell a quotation from a paraphrase built from the same words. A passage that
does not verify is marked `verified = FALSE` and counted in
`ans$notes$unverified_evidence`, and any one of them makes the answer partial.

`gr_read_spec(verify = TRUE)` runs the same check inside `gr_read()`: it writes
the check's columns onto `$evidence`, marks the answer partial when a quotation
is not found, counts the quotations it checked in `notes$quotes_checked`, and
records a `read.verify` step in the trace. It also holds `iterative` to
quoting: each step must list the passages its answer rests on, word for word
with their chunk numbers, and the loop stops only when every one is found in the
chunk it names. A run that ends with none accepted keeps the refused answer in
`notes$unverified_answer` and reports the answer as not in the document.

```{r}
vspec <- gr_read_spec(reader = "skim", verify = TRUE)
checked <- gr_read(chunks, "What was revenue in 2024?", gr_mock_client(stand_in), vspec)
checked$notes$quotes_checked
checked$evidence[, c("verified", "match", "quote_status", "quote_sim")]
```

The last columns come from a second matcher, recorded beside `verified`:
`quote_status`, `quote_sim`, `quote_coverage`, `quote_edits` and
`quote_critical_ok`. It expands ligatures, joins words hyphenated across a line,
and scores the closest window of the source by character edits, with numbers
and negations required to be identical. Its statuses are `verbatim`,
`near_verbatim`, `unverified`, and `not_checked` for a passage too long to
score. On a labelled set of 343 true and 162 false quotations it rejects 1.2% of
true ones, against 36.4% for the existing check, and accepts none with a changed
digit, number word, comparison sign or negation. It does accept 25 of 46
quotations with one content word swapped as `near_verbatim`, so it decides
nothing in this release: `verified` and `match` still decide.

The other columns of `ans$evidence` are `page`, filled in only for a PDF,
`section`, `kind`, and `score`, which only `retrieve` (similarity) and
`rerank` (the model's 0 to 10) set. This check and the citation check above are
string comparisons on text you already have, so they cost nothing and always
run.

## Questions that assume something false

A question can take for granted something the document contradicts: "Why did
revenue fall in 2024?" of a report in which revenue rose. A reader then either
answers on the question's terms or says the answer is not in the document, and
either way what the document does say is lost. With `premise = TRUE` in
`gr_read_spec()`, the model is told that if the excerpts state the opposite of
something the question assumes, it should say so in one sentence and give what
they state instead. That sentence is `ans$answer` and `ans$premise`, and
`is_not_found()` is `FALSE` for it. Excerpts that are merely silent still count
as not found.

A reader that answers in one request (`stuff`, `retrieve`, `rerank`, `skim`,
`hierarchical`, `preview`) gives that request's verdict. `map_reduce` passes a
chunk that contradicts the question to its merge as a finding, and
`ans$notes$premise_chunks` lists the chunks that said so, whatever the merge
decided; `ensemble` does the same with its members
(`ans$notes$premise_members`). `?gr_read_spec` describes the rest.

This stand-in plays a model that finds the summary contradicts the question and
the other chunks silent. `FALSE_PREMISE:` is how the model is asked to open such
a reply:

```{r}
loaded <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  sent <- paste(vapply(messages[-1], function(m) m$content, character(1)),
                collapse = "\n")
  if (grepl("45.2 million", sent, fixed = TRUE)) {
    return("FALSE_PREMISE: Revenue rose to 45.2 million dollars, from 38.7 million.")
  }
  "NOT_IN_DOCUMENT"
})
ans <- gr_read(chunks, "Why did revenue fall in 2024?", loaded,
               gr_read_spec("map_reduce", premise = TRUE))
ans$premise
is_not_found(ans$answer)
ans$notes$premise_chunks
```

The verdict is the model's reading of the excerpts, not something harnessr checks,
so weigh it as you would any answer. The check is off by default because it
makes the prompts longer, so a cache or a recorded run made without it does not
answer a run with it. `extract` and `screen` ignore it.

## Trying readers on your own documents

The best way to choose is to test on a few documents where you already know the
answer. `gr_compare()` runs several configurations on one document, extracting the
text once and sharing chunks between configurations that cut them the same way:

```{r}
cmp <- gr_compare(gr_example(), "What was revenue in 2024?", list(
  gr_recipe("narrow", segment = list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120),
            read = list(reader = "retrieve", top_k = 2)),
  gr_recipe("wide", segment = list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120),
            read = list(reader = "retrieve", top_k = 6)),
  gr_recipe("all", segment = list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120),
            read = list(reader = "map_reduce"))),
  client = gr_mock_client(stand_in))
cmp$summary[, c("recipe", "reader", "settings", "chunks_used", "not_found", "partial")]
```

`settings` names whatever each configuration changed from the defaults, so rows
that differ only in a number can be told apart. Two configurations that would do
exactly the same work are run once, with a warning, rather than paid for twice.

## When a provider cannot do structured replies

`rerank`, `iterative` and `preview` ask the model to reply in a fixed structure
(JSON), which most current providers support. Where the structure is not supported
or the reply cannot be read, each one falls back, warns, and marks the answer
partial: `rerank` to word-matching order, `iterative` to a single retrieval,
`preview` to reading everything. The answer is still produced; `partial` tells
you it came by the fallback.

Every call that asks for JSON (these three, model segmentation, screening,
claims, outlines and extraction) checks the reply's types, `enum` values and
`required` fields, through nested objects and arrays, before using it. A reply
that fails is treated as one that did not parse: the reader takes its failure
path, the reply is not cached, and the reason says where the reply broke the
schema, as in `$.groups[0]: expected array, got 1`. `gr_extract()` still reads
each field's value itself, so "1,204" in an integer field is still 1204; only
the shape of its replies is checked.

## When the answer is not what you expected

The answer object and its trace record enough to find the cause without
guessing. In order of how often each is the cause:

| symptom | check | likely cause |
|---|---|---|
| `NOT_IN_DOCUMENT`, but you can see the answer in the file | `nrow(ans$evidence)`, then `gr_chunk_stats()` | the chunk holding it never reached the model. Lower `max_tokens`, raise `top_k`, or switch to a reader whose `signature` starts `all\|` |
| the answer is right but thin | `ans$notes$chunks` against `length(ans$chunks_used)` | most chunks answered `NOT_IN_DOCUMENT`. That is usually correct; if not, the chunk boundaries are cutting the evidence in half, so add `overlap_tokens` (`vignette("segment")`) |
| `ans$partial` is `TRUE` | `print(ans)`, then `ans$notes` and `print(ans$trace)` | `failed_calls` (transport), `dropped_chunks` (did not fit), `call_cap_reached` or `cost_cap_reached` (`vignette("runs")`), `unread_pages` (no text layer and no OCR), or a merge that fell back to joining the answers |
| `ans$notes$unverified_evidence` is set | `gr_verify_evidence(ans)` | the model wrote a quotation that is not in the chunk it is attributed to. `match` says how far off: near 1 is a typo, near 0 is invention |
| `ans$notes$cited_unknown` is set | that value against `ans$chunks_used` | the answer cited a chunk that was never sent to it |
| figures, dates or percentages are missing | `doc$stats$clean_log` | a cleaning step removed them. `remove_numbers` is off by default; the `legacy` preset turns it on (`vignette("ingest")`) |
| a scanned PDF comes back nearly empty | `doc$stats$chars` and `doc$stats$unread_pages`, and any `gr_ocr_unavailable` warning | OCR did not run or is not installed. Force it with `gr_ingest_spec(ocr = "always")`, and check `tesseract` and `magick` are present |
| every chunk is the whole document | `nrow(doc$blocks)` | the file has no blank lines between paragraphs, so there is nothing to split on. Use `method = "sentence"` or `"fixed"` |
| the run costs far more than expected | `gr_readers()$cost_calls` | the reader makes one request per chunk and `max_tokens` is small. Run `gr_chunk_stats()` first; it is free |
| answers change between identical runs | the `temperature` setting, unset by default | set `temperature = 0`. Reasoning models ignore it (`gr_model_info(m)$supports_temperature`) |
| `NOT_IN_DOCUMENT` for a question that assumes something the document contradicts | `ans$premise`, with `premise = TRUE` | without the check a reader can only answer or say the excerpts are silent; see "Questions that assume something false" above |

Test for the marker with `is_not_found(ans$answer)` rather than
`grepl("NOT_IN_DOCUMENT", ...)`: a real answer can quote the marker, and models
decorate it (`**NOT_IN_DOCUMENT.**`).

Two habits make all of this cheaper: run `gr_chunk_stats()` before you spend
anything, and keep `gr_options(max_cost_usd = ...)` set to something you would
not mind paying by accident.

## Choosing the settings

Each walkthrough below takes one reading setting or group: what it controls
and what it trades off, the signs in your results that point to changing it,
where its default came from, and how to test a change. `vignette("settings")`
lists every reading setting with its default, and `gr_settings("read")` gives
each one's evidence.

The tests use `hr_sweep()`, which builds one arm per value of a setting, and
`hr_benchmark()`, which runs the arms on a reference. Here they run on one
question about the example report and the stand-in model above, so they show
what each value sends and what `hr_sweep_check()` reports, not which value
answers better. `vignette("compare")` sweeps `top_k` on a reference of 32
questions with dev and test splits and reads the result with intervals.

```{r}
qa <- gr_qa_reference(questions = c(revenue = "What was revenue in 2024?"),
                      documents = gr_example(), answers = list("45.2 million"),
                      split = "dev")
reads <- gr_mock_client(stand_in)
sweep <- function(arms) {
  hr_benchmark(arms, qa, runs = 5, client = reads, split = "dev",
               scorer = gr_scorer_answer())
}
calls <- function(bench) {
  vapply(attr(bench, "traces")[bench$ledger_id], function(t) nrow(as.data.frame(t)),
         integer(1))
}
```

### Which reader {#set-reader}

**What it controls.** The reader decides how the chunks reach the model (see
"The readers" above). The main trade is between readers that send every chunk
(`map_reduce`, `refine`, `hierarchical`, `skim`), whose cost grows with the
document and which cannot miss a chunk, and readers that pick a few
(`retrieve`, `rerank`, `iterative`), whose cost does not grow with the
document and which answer only from what they picked. Among the first group,
`map_reduce` reads each chunk alone, `refine` carries a draft through the
document in order, `hierarchical` answers from summaries, and `skim` answers
from passages it quotes, which `verify` can check. `skim_model` and
`summary_model` put the per-chunk work of `skim` and `hierarchical` on a
cheaper model.

**Signs it needs changing.** `NOT_IN_DOCUMENT` from `retrieve` for a fact you
can find in the file, with `ans$evidence` holding other chunks, means the pick
missed: try a reader that sends every chunk, or `rerank`. A bill that grows
with every page added, for one-fact questions, points the other way. An answer
that misses how an argument develops points to `refine`; one that needs
exact wording to `skim`.

**Where the default came from.** `gr_read_spec()` defaults to `map_reduce`,
chosen because it reads the whole document at any length; no comparison of
readers is recorded (`untested`). `answer_document()` chooses `"fast"` or
`"thorough"` by length (`auto_max_tokens` in `gr_options()`).

**How to test it.** Sweep the reader on one segmentation:

```{r}
base <- gr_arm("thorough", list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120,
                                overlap_tokens = 0))
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(base, list(reader = c("map_reduce", "refine", "hierarchical",
                                              "skim", "retrieve"))))
bench$calls <- calls(bench)
aggregate(cbind(calls, tokens_in) ~ param.reader, bench, mean)
```

On eight chunks the four readers that send every chunk make 8 or 9 requests
and send 1273 to 1839 prompt tokens; `retrieve` makes one request of 584.
`refine` sends the most because every request carries the draft so far.

### How many chunks: `top_k` and `min_score` {#set-top-k}

**What it controls.** `top_k` is how many chunks `retrieve` and `rerank` send,
and how many `iterative` adds each round. More chunks make it likelier the
answer is among them, and make the prompt longer and the answer's evidence
noisier. `min_score` drops chunks less similar to the question than a floor,
keeping the best one.

**Signs it needs changing.** `NOT_IN_DOCUMENT` where `ans$evidence` holds
chunks next to the one with the answer points to a larger `top_k`, and so does
`gr_seg_recall()` finding the answer at rank 5 when `top_k` is 4. An answer
built from several unrelated chunks, or a cost per question far above what
one fact needs, points to a smaller one.

**Where the default came from.** 6, a common starting value for retrieval,
not tuned here (`untested`). `"needle"` uses 8.

**How to test it.**

```{r}
needle <- gr_arm("needle", list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120))
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(needle, list(top_k = c(2, 4, 8, 12))))
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.top_k, bench, mean)
```

The prompt grows from 289 tokens at `top_k = 2` to 909 at 12. In
`vignette("compare")` a `top_k` sweep on a different arm, the `"fast"` recipe
with the `retrieve` reader and 40-token sentence chunks, found `top_k = 2` more
accurate than 4 on 32 test questions, with an interval from 1.8 to 12.0
points, and cheaper. That result is for its arm and its stand-in model; yours
is found the same way.

### Diversity: `mmr` {#set-mmr}

**What it controls.** Below 1, `mmr` trades relevance for diversity when
`retrieve` and `iterative` pick chunks, so near-duplicates do not fill every
place (see "Choosing and placing chunks" above). It costs nothing.

**Signs it needs changing.** `ans$evidence` holding several chunks that say
the same thing, from a document that repeats itself (an abstract, a summary,
a conclusion), points to `mmr` below 1. Answers that miss the best chunk after
lowering it point back up.

**Where the default came from.** 1, plain top-k, the selection used before
the setting existed (`untested`). 0.7 is a common starting point for a
balance.

**How to test it.**

```{r}
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(needle, expand.grid(top_k = 3, mmr = c(1, 0.7, 0.3))))
hr_sweep_check(bench)
```

At 0.7 the three chunks picked were the ones plain top-k picked, so the
requests were the same; only 0.3 changed them on this report. A sweep of
`mmr` is worth running only on documents that repeat themselves, and
`hr_sweep_check()` says when it reached none.

### Word matching: `lexical_blend`, `bm25_k1` and `bm25_b` {#set-lexical}

**What they control.** With lexical embeddings (`gr_options(embedder =
"lexical")`), `retrieve` scores chunks by a blend of cosine similarity and
BM25, with `lexical_blend` the weight on cosine. `bm25_k1` sets how fast
repeated words stop adding to a chunk's score, and `bm25_b` how much long
chunks are penalised; `rerank` uses BM25 to choose its candidates.

**Signs they need changing.** Retrieval that picks long chunks which mention
the question's words once each, over a short chunk that answers it, points to
a higher `bm25_b` or a lower `lexical_blend`. With real embeddings these
settings do nothing for `retrieve`, and `hr_sweep_check()` shows it.

**Where the defaults came from.** Robertson and Zaragoza (2009) give
`bm25_b = 0.75` as the usual value and `bm25_k1` between 1.2 and 2.0; 1.5 lies
inside that range (`cited`). Neither was tuned here. `lexical_blend = 0.5`,
an even blend, was set when the offline path was written (`untested`).

**How to test them.**

```{r}
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(needle, expand.grid(top_k = 2, lexical_blend = c(0, 0.5, 1))))
hr_sweep_check(bench)
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(needle, expand.grid(top_k = 3, bm25_b = c(0.75, 0.3))))
hr_sweep_check(bench)
```

Each value of `lexical_blend` picked different chunks here, while `bm25_b` at
0.3 picked the same three as at 0.75.

### Placement: `context_order` and `restate` {#set-context-order}

**What they control.** `context_order` puts the chosen chunks in order of
relevance, in document order, or with the best at the two ends of the prompt
(`"edges"`). `restate` repeats the question before the excerpts; under
`"auto"` that happens when they are longer than `restate_tokens` (1200). Both
change only where text sits, not which text is sent, and `restate` adds the
question's length to each request.

**Signs they need changing.** Right answers from short prompts and misses from
long ones, with the answer's chunk sent each time, point to placement:
`"edges"`, or `restate = "always"`. Answers that misread chunks that follow on
from each other point to `"document"`.

**Where the defaults came from.** `"relevance"` is the order the readers used
before the setting existed; the alternatives were added to be compared, and no
comparison is recorded. `restate = "auto"` was added so a comparison could
measure it, and nothing has. `restate_tokens = 1200` is an arbitrary number,
kept from when it was a constant. Both are `untested`.

**How to test them.**

```{r}
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(needle, expand.grid(top_k = 3,
                                            context_order = c("relevance", "edges", "document"),
                                            restate = c("never", "always"))))
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.context_order + param.restate, bench, mean)
hr_sweep_check(bench)
```

Repeating the question added 11 prompt tokens per request. `"document"` sent
what `"relevance"` sent, because the three chunks chosen were already in
document order; `"edges"` changed the requests.

### Checking the answer: `verify` and `cite` {#set-verify}

**What they control.** `cite = TRUE` asks the model to cite the chunks it
used (see "Asking for citations"), which lengthens the prompt a little and
lets a citation to a chunk never sent be caught. `verify = TRUE` checks each
quotation in the answer against the chunk it names, after the reply, and marks
the answer partial when one is not found (see "Checking what an answer rests
on"); under `iterative` it also requires quotations before the loop may stop.
`accept_near_verbatim` lets a near-verbatim quotation count there.

**Signs they are needed.** Answers you cannot trace to a page, or a reviewer
asking where a figure came from, point to `cite`. Any answer you will act on
without reading the source points to `verify`; so does a reader that quotes
(`skim`), whose quotations are the model's words until checked.

**Where the defaults came from.** Both are off, so a run sends the requests and
accepts the answers it did before they existed (`untested`).
`accept_near_verbatim` is off as well; on the labelled quotation set, 25 of 46
quotations with one content word swapped score `near_verbatim`.

**How to test them.**

```{r}
precise <- gr_arm("precise", list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120,
                                  overlap_tokens = 0))
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(precise, expand.grid(cite = c(FALSE, TRUE), verify = c(FALSE, TRUE))))
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.cite + param.verify, bench, mean)
hr_sweep_check(bench)
```

`cite` added 22 prompt tokens to each run. `verify` sent the same requests as
no check, as it should: it acts on the reply, so its effect is in which
answers are marked partial (`ans$partial`, `ans$notes$unverified_evidence`),
not in what is sent. Score it with a scorer that counts a partial answer as
wrong, or compare the `partial` rate by hand.

### Reasoning: `effort` {#set-effort}

**What it controls.** `effort` sets how much a reasoning model reasons, for
every request or by stage (see "Reasoning effort, stage by stage"). Reasoning
is billed as output and shares the reply's cap, so lower effort is cheaper and
faster, and higher effort can help the few requests that judge or combine.

**Signs it needs changing.** `tokens_reasoning` in a benchmark, or the trace,
taking most of the output of per-chunk requests points to `"low"` for those
stages. A reply cut off (`finish_reason = "length"`) at `"high"` needs a larger
`max_answer_tokens`. Merges or final answers that miss what the per-chunk
answers found point to more effort at `reduce` or `*.answer`.

**Where the default came from.** Unset: no effort is sent, and the provider's
own default applies (`untested`). `?gr_read_spec` gives a starting profile,
low for the many mechanical requests and high for the few that judge, which is
not a measured default.

**How to test it.** Effort is sent only to a model harnessr lists as a
reasoning model, so the arms name one. A map goes in a list column:

```{r}
luna <- gr_arm("thorough", list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120,
                                overlap_tokens = 0, model = "gpt-5.6-luna"))
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(luna, data.frame(effort = I(list(
  "low", c(map = "low", reduce = "high"), "high")))))
unique(bench$arm)
```

Compare `usd`, `tokens_reasoning` and `correct` by `param.effort` on your own
reference. The stand-in model reports no reasoning tokens, so here only the
requests differ.

### Merges: `max_merge_levels` {#set-merge-levels}

**What it controls.** When the findings of `map_reduce`, `skim` and the other
merging readers do not fit one merge request, they are merged in levels.
`max_merge_levels` caps the levels; past it the reader returns its findings
unmerged and cut, and marks the answer partial. `fan_in` and `max_levels` play
the same parts for `hierarchical`'s summaries.

**Signs it needs changing.** A partial answer whose notes say a merge fell back
to joining the answers, on a very long document, points to a higher cap (or to
larger chunks, which make fewer findings). A cost dominated by `reduce`
requests points to a lower one.

**Where the default came from.** 6, the cap the merge code had as a constant;
not tuned (`untested`).

**How to test it.**

```{r}
bench <- sweep(hr_sweep(base, list(max_merge_levels = c(1, 6))))
hr_sweep_check(bench)
```

Eight findings merge in one level, so a cap of 1 sent the same requests as 6
on this report. Test the cap on your longest documents, where it can bind.

### Preview safeguards: `unskip_k` and `reread_on` {#set-preview}

**What they control.** `preview` follows a plan its first request makes, and
a section the plan skips is never read. `unskip_k` reads the `k` sections
that match the question's words best (BM25 over each section's text) even
when the plan skips them, so a plan cannot drop the one section that holds
the question's words; it costs no request, but the answer prompt grows by the
sections it adds. `reread_on = "not_found"` follows an answer of
`NOT_IN_DOCUMENT` with one more request over the sections not read in full,
so it trades at most one request for a second look. Every skip is in the
trace as a `preview.skip` step with its score, whatever the settings.

**Signs they need changing.** `NOT_IN_DOCUMENT` from `preview` for a fact
you can find, where `ans$notes$plan` shows its section skipped, or a
`preview.skip` step in the trace with a high score, points to `unskip_k = 1`.
Not-found answers on questions you know the document answers point to
`reread_on = "not_found"`.

**Where the defaults came from.** Both are off (`unskip_k = 0`,
`reread_on = "never"`), so `preview` makes the requests it made before they
existed (`untested`).

**How to test them.** Here the plan skips the summary, which holds the
revenue figure:

```{r}
skips_summary <- function(messages, params) {
  if (identical(params$schema_name, "reading_plan")) {
    return(paste0('{"sections": [{"id": 1, "treatment": "read", "reason": "Title."}, ',
                  '{"id": 2, "treatment": "skip", "reason": "A summary repeats."}]}'))
  }
  stand_in(messages, params)
}
looks <- gr_arm("thorough", list(method = "structural", max_tokens = 120,
                                 overlap_tokens = 0, reader = "preview"))
bench <- hr_benchmark(hr_sweep(looks, expand.grid(unskip_k = c(0, 1),
                                                  reread_on = c("never", "not_found"))),
                      qa, runs = 5, client = gr_mock_client(skips_summary), split = "dev",
                      scorer = gr_scorer_answer())
aggregate(tokens_in ~ param.unskip_k + param.reread_on, bench, mean)
hr_sweep_check(bench)
```

`unskip_k = 1` put the summary back into the answer prompt, 106 prompt
tokens more. `reread_on` sent nothing more here, because the stand-in model
never answers `NOT_IN_DOCUMENT`, and `hr_sweep_check()` lists those arms as
sending the same requests as the arms without it. Test it on questions your
reader misses.

gr_options(old)
